cue.topic: Describe a memorable journey you have made
bullets: and explain why it was so memorable

part2.model: I'd like to talk about a train journey I made across Vietnam two summers ago, from Hanoi down to Ho Chi Minh City. I travelled with my cousin Priya, who had always dreamed of seeing the country from a train window, so we booked a sleeper cabin and set off early one morning in July. The trip took almost two days, and we stopped in Hue and Da Nang along the way. What made it so memorable was the scenery. The line runs along the coast in places, so we were gazing out at turquoise water and sweeping rice fields for hours on end. Halfway through, we got chatting to an elderly couple who shared their home-made snacks with us and taught us a few phrases in Vietnamese. That was a real highlight. Of course, it wasn't all smooth sailing. The air conditioning broke down in the middle of the night, and we were stuck in a stuffy compartment until dawn. Looking back, though, it only added to the adventure, and we still laugh about it. I'd say the journey was memorable because it was so far removed from my normal routine. Instead of rushing from one landmark to the next, we simply slowed down and soaked up the atmosphere. It made me realise that sometimes the journey matters more than the destination, and I've been keen to travel by rail ever since.

vocab.example: We set off at dawn to avoid the heavy motorway traffic.

questions.q: Why do so many people like to travel abroad nowadays?
questions.model: Mainly because travel has become far more accessible. Budget airlines and online booking have brought prices down, so a weekend abroad is within reach for many families. Beyond that, people crave new experiences and want to broaden their horizons, particularly after spending most of the week at a desk. Personally, I think seeing other cultures makes us more open-minded, although it's worth noting that some people simply travel for the photos.

In my view, governments should encourage visitors to use locally owned businesses, so that the money stays in the community and residents genuinely benefit from the visitors who arrive.

questions.q: What might be the negative effects of mass tourism on popular destinations?
questions.model: Overcrowding is the obvious one. Places like Venice are overrun with visitors, which pushes up rents and forces local people out of their own neighbourhoods. There is also the environmental cost, as litter and emissions can damage fragile coastlines. Some argue that tourists spoil the very places they come to admire. I'd say the solution is to limit numbers and charge entry fees, so that the damage is kept in check and the money funds conservation.

questions.q: Should governments do more to protect historical sites from damage by visitors?
questions.model: Yes, I believe they should, because these places are irreplaceable. Once an ancient carving is worn away, no amount of money can bring it back. Governments could introduce timed tickets, ban flash photography and fund proper restoration work. Admittedly, that costs money, but heritage is part of a nation's identity, and future generations deserve to see it. In the long run, protecting these sites also keeps tourism alive, which benefits everyone.

questions.q: What might travel look like in fifty years' time?
questions.model: It's hard to predict, but I suspect it will be greener and more automated. Electric planes and high-speed rail could cut emissions dramatically, while virtual reality might let people explore a destination before they even book. Space tourism may become a reality for the very wealthy too, though I doubt it will ever go mainstream. What I hope is that travel remains about real human encounters rather than just ticking off landmarks.

questions.q: Would you say independent travel is better than going on a package tour?
questions.model: It depends on the traveller. Package tours are stress-free because everything is arranged, which suits families and first-time visitors. On the other hand, independent travel gives you the freedom to wander off and follow your curiosity. Personally, I'd go for the latter, since the unplanned moments are usually the best ones, although I'd book the first night's accommodation just to avoid arriving with nowhere to stay. Either way, the best trips leave room for surprises.
